Q: HTML multipart/form-data form submits correctly except on iOS, where $_POST and $_FILES are empty when a file is attached A:

Before blaming WebKit, check post_max_size.

If the request body is larger than post_max_size, PHP discards the whole thing: $_POST and $_FILES both come back empty, there is no error code left in $_FILES either, and the only trace is a "POST Content-Length ... exceeds the limit" line in the PHP error log. This is documented behaviour, see the note under post_max_size in the manual: https://www.php.net/manual/en/ini.core.php#ini.post-max-size

It reads as iOS-only because of what the device attaches. A photo taken on an iPhone 16 Pro Max is a 48MP HEIC in the 5-15 MB range, while whatever you picked from a desktop was probably a few hundred KB, so the same form stays under the limit everywhere else.

Check the PHP error log for that line first, then compare the phone's actual file size against php -i | grep -E 'post_max_size|upload_max_filesize|memory_limit'. post_max_size has to exceed upload_max_filesize, and memory_limit has to exceed post_max_size, otherwise you only move where it breaks (same manual page, and https://www.php.net/manual/en/features.file-upload.common-pitfalls.php).

If the limits are already generous, the next suspects sit in front of PHP and give the identical symptom: nginx client_max_body_size (https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_core_module.html#client_max_body_size), the equivalent LiteSpeed request body limit, or mod_security dropping the body. Those leave a 413 or 403 in the web server access log while the browser still renders your page, so read that log too, not only PHP's.

One iOS-specific detail worth ruling out while you are there: with Live Photos on, Safari can attach the paired .mov as well, so a "3 MB photo" arrives heavier than the gallery claims.Before blaming WebKit, check post_max_size.

It reads as iOS-only because of what the device attaches. A photo taken on an iPhone 16 Pro Max is a 48MP HEIC somewhere in the 5-15 MB range, while whatever you picked from the desktop was probably a few hundred KB.

So: look in the PHP error log for that line, then compare php -i | grep -E 'post_max_size|upload_max_filesize|memory_limit' with the actual file size coming off the phone. post_max_size has to be bigger than upload_max_filesize, and memory_limit bigger than post_max_size, otherwise you only move where it breaks.

If the limits are already generous, the next suspects sit in front of PHP and produce the identical symptom: nginx client_max_body_size, LiteSpeed's request body limit, or mod_security dropping the body. Those leave a 413 or 403 in the web server access log while the browser still renders your page, so check that log as well, not only PHP's.

One more iOS-specific detail worth ruling out: if Live Photos are enabled, Safari can attach the paired .mov as well, so a "3 MB photo" arrives noticeably heavier than the gallery says.

Q: RGB to hex and hex to RGB A:

Uint8Array methods

The Uint8Array typed array represents an array of 8-bit unsigned integers ranging from 0 to 255. You can use the fromHex() and toHex() methods of Uint8Array. These methods are concise and less error-prone than manual string parsing or bitwise operations.

Hex to RGB

The Uint8Array.fromHex() static method creates a new Uint8Array object from a hexadecimal string. This method parses the string into a byte array.

const [r, g, b] = Uint8Array.fromHex('ffffff');
console.log(`rgb(${r}, ${g}, ${b})`);

RGB to hex

The toHex() method of Uint8Array instances returns a hex-encoded string based on the data in this Uint8Array object. This method creates strings from a byte array.

const bytes = new Uint8Array([255, 255, 255]);
console.log('#' + bytes.toHex());

Q: Random color generator A:

High-quality randomness

You can use the the Web Crypto API.

RGB color

The Uint8Array typed array represents an array of 8-bit unsigned integers ranging from 0 to 255:

const [r, g, b] = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(3));
console.log(`rgb(${r}, ${g}, ${b})`);

Hex color

You can also use the toHex() method of Uint8Array instances:

const bytes = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(3));
console.log('#' + bytes.toHex());

A demo on my website: Random Background Color

Q: How long will take Bubble sort with array of 1 000 000 ints? A:

Big-O notation is good when answering the question "as the size of the problem goes up, how does the time/memory needed to solve it grow?". It purposefully ignores all "small" details, and considers an algorithm A that uses 10x (or 100000x - any constant ratio) more time than another algorithm B to be equivalent. In real life, of course, 10x performance does matter. So the 1st problem is that O(n^2) ignores all constant factors (but real-world time does not).

Using the (currently 1st pseudocode example) wikipedia version of Bubblesort:

procedure bubbleSort(A : list of sortable items)
    n := length(A)
    repeat
        swapped := false
        for i := 1 to n - 1 inclusive do
            if A[i - 1] > A[i] then
                swap(A[i - 1], A[i])
                swapped = true
            end if
        end for
        n := n - 1
    until not swapped
end procedure

you can see that there will be 0 swaps if all elements are initially sorted. Any modern computer implementing this pseudo-code will be able to "sort" an already-sorted array of 1M integers in less than 1 second. So the 2nd problem is that (most implementations, including the above) of bubble-sort are much faster if the array is almost ordered. It so happens that, in real life, arrays are a bit more ordered than what one would expect from a random sampling - which leads to real-world sorting algorithms looking for shortcuts to exploit this.

And of course, the 3rd problem (after looking at what big-O ignores about the code and the exact degree of disorder in the array) has to do with the detailed characteristics of the platform that you execute your code on, and exactly what machine-level instructions you execute on that platform. If, for example, all your data fits into the machine's caches (thus avoiding costly repeated access to main memory), further efficiency can be gained -- at a level that is mostly independent of the algorithm's implementation.

If you look at real-world benchmarks, they specify in full detail all 3 aspects: exact code used, exact data input, and exact compiler & machine architecture. Note that, even then, it is not easy to predict how the run-time will increase as program-size increases, because many transitions will be in the form of steps due to data no longer fitting inside slower memory, rather than smooth increases.

TLDR: the only safe estimate is to measure the time. And it will only answer the question for your implementation, chosen input, & machine. Failing that, you can do several smaller runs, fit a parabola to your data, and extrapolate the result to size 1M: it will not be far off the mark, as 1M ints is not that much.

Q: Can C++ "happens-before" order contradict physical wall-clock execution time? A:

Yes, it can. The key distinction is that C++ happens-before is a logical ordering relation, not a statement about physical wall-clock timing. An operation can be ordered before another by the language memory model even when the actual execution or observation timing looks different due to compiler reordering, CPU out-of-order execution, caching, or synchronization. So “A happens-before B” should be read as a guarantee about permitted program behavior and visibility—not as “A physically occurred earlier on a clock.”
